weakness: The pipeline reduced the tool's detected 3D orientation to a single yaw angle and hard-coded which side of the handle the hook is on. When the tool lay flipped over (a mirror image in the table plane, yaw still ~0), it put the handle on the wrong side of the cube and lowered the hook into empty table, so the pull never touched the cube (0/10).
how_found: Questioned A1 (the tool lies upright, so yaw describes it). The first attempt at this round, a 180-degree yaw of the tool, was rejected by the break gate (0.9), which showed yaw was already handled; flipping is the orientation change that yaw cannot see.
why_missed: In every default episode the tool spawns upright with the same face up, so a yaw-only model of its pose was always right and the hook side looked like a constant of the task.
fix: detect_avg now returns the full rotation (chordal mean of the noisy detection rotations, projected back with SVD). The hook direction is read from the full rotation (sign of the tool's +y axis after rotating the handle to world +x), the handle is placed on the opposite side of the cube from the hook, and the hand-to-tool transform and target pose use the full rotation instead of a yaw-only quaternion.
general_rule: Derive the direction of every functional feature of an object (hook, opening, handle side) from its full detected 3D rotation, never from yaw alone or from the side it usually faces, since objects can be lying flipped or mirrored.

weakness: The cube was detected once at the very start and the hook was placed from that stale estimate about 10 s later. When the cube was pushed 13 cm sideways while the robot fetched the tool, the hook came down where the cube used to be and the pull dragged nothing (0/10). While repairing, a second weakness appeared on the base task: the tool, gripped near its end with the hook mass 17 cm away, pivoted up to 35 deg in the fingers during the fast carry, so the drooping hook swept the table and knocked the cube out of reach; the in-hand pose measured once after the lift was then wrong.
how_found: Questioned A8 (objects stay where they were first seen), because the target is acted on long after it is perceived and on a real table things get bumped. A first design with a 1.5 cm push was rejected by the break gate (1.0): the placement clearances absorbed it, so the push had to exceed the clearance to test the assumption.
why_missed: In the default task nothing moves, so one detection at the start was always still valid, and the initial grasp of the tool happened to hold it rigidly enough at the default speeds in the 10 evaluation seeds.
fix: Before placing the tool, hold still until two consecutive half-second windows of cube detections agree within 1.2 cm, then re-detect the cube (20 averaged detections) and plan the hook placement from that. Carry the held tool at slow speed, re-measure the tool-in-hand transform after every carry (after lift, after transfer, after lowering), and compute the hand pose so that the tool itself is level (target orientation of the tool, not of the hand).
general_rule: Re-perceive every object right before the step that depends on its pose (and wait until it is still), and after picking up anything that is used to act on the world, re-measure its pose in the hand after each carry and command the held object's pose rather than the hand's.

weakness: The pull went straight back along -x with no knowledge of other objects, so an immovable block right behind the cube jammed it (0/10). The first repair also showed that the obstacle check must include the gripper itself: the 0.2 m-wide hand (along the finger axis) came down on top of the block while the handle was being lowered beside the cube, and the tool was knocked out of the fingers.
how_found: Questioned A9 (the straight path from the cube to the goal is free), the assumption a cluttered real table most often violates.
why_missed: The default scene contains only the tool and the cube, so no path was ever blocked and get_obstacles() was never called.
fix: Kept for later rounds: read get_obstacles(), check the swept footprint of tool, cube AND hand (real hand box measured from the robot's collision geometry) along each candidate stroke, and choose a plan from: straight pull, sideways detour pushed by the handle then pull, and a tilted tool that raises the hand. Not recovered: with the cube 0.83 m from the base and the block directly behind it, every configuration that avoids sweeping the long handle into the block needs the hand 0.82-0.88 m from the base, beyond the arm's ~0.80 m reach at table height. Oracle also 0.0. Marked unsolved and replaced by v4 (block further back in the lane).
general_rule: Collision-check the whole swept volume of every stroke, including your own hand and the held tool, against all perceived obstacles before executing it, and verify a detour stays within the arm's reach.

weakness: Same as v3 in a solvable layout: an immovable block halfway down the straight pull lane; the round-2 pipeline pulled the cube straight into it (0/10).
how_found: v3 attacked A9 but was not solvable within reach; v4 moves the block (and the fixed cube spot) so a detour exists. It is labelled parameter_tuning because only the positions changed relative to v3.
why_missed: See v3: the default scene never blocks the lane.
fix: The obstacle-aware planner written during v3: averaged get_obstacles() boxes, swept-footprint check (tool parts, cube, hand + fingers; 7 mm margin for tool/cube, 15 mm for the hand), plans tried in order of how unusual they are (straight pull, then sideways handle push of increasing length then pull, then the same with the tool tilted to raise the hand), vertical descent also checked. Here it picks a 0.22 m sideways push and then the pull. Note: this fix was written during the v3 attempt; the v4 gate measured the committed round-2 pipeline (s_break 0.0).
general_rule: When the direct path to the goal is blocked, search over a small set of motion primitives (push sideways, then pull) and execute the cheapest sequence whose full swept footprint is collision-free.

weakness: The pipeline always lifted and carried the tool by its free end. With a tool twice as heavy (1.0 kg) the gravity torque exceeded the grip friction, the tool swung to ~45 deg in the fingers, its drooping hook knocked the cube away during the carry, and the placement computed for a level tool was wrong (0/10). The repair also exposed two latent weaknesses: contact moves that fail the straight-line planner silently fell back to RRT (which lifted the tool off the cube mid-pull), and waypoints were chosen without checking that they were within the arm's reach (one episode spent 1400 steps on an unreachable waypoint).
how_found: Questioned A10 (the held tool is rigid in the hand). A sweep showed that a heavy or high-friction cube (2 kg, mu 2) and a slippery tool did not break the pipeline, but a heavier tool did, because it is held 12 cm from its centre of mass.
why_missed: With the default 0.5 kg tool the pivot is only ~5 deg at slow speed, so lifting by the end looked safe; the reach limit and the RRT fallback never showed because the default placements happened to be reachable along straight lines.
fix: Test lift: after lifting, measure how much the tool hangs in the fingers; if more than 12 deg, put it back down and slide it on the table (the table carries its weight) to a pre-hook pose beside the cube, then sideways into the hooking pose, with the slide route checked against the cube and obstacles. All contact moves (slide, sideways push, pull) are split into 4 cm straight hops. The tool is laid and pulled along the radial direction from the robot base to the cube, and every plan and route is checked against a reach limit (0.80 m from the base).
general_rule: After grasping an object you will use as a tool, do a test lift and measure how much it slips or pivots in the grip; if it does, keep it supported (slide it) or regrasp nearer its centre of mass, and make every contact move short straight segments within verified reach.

weakness: The tool was always grasped top-down at one fixed point 2.5 cm from the handle's free end, at a hard-coded table-level height. With a 15 cm tall bottle-sized block standing right beside that end of the handle, the open fingers and the 0.2 m-wide hand came down onto the block, so the grasp failed or knocked the tool away (0/10). The oracle also failed (0.0).
how_found: Questioned A3 and A4 (the tool rests on the table and its fixed grasp point is free). A first design that raised the tool on a 6 cm platform (attacking A3) was rejected by the break gate (1.0): the hand's compliance still produced a grasp at the wrong height. That showed the height was not the weak point, but the fixed grasp location was, so v6 blocks the approach to that location instead.
why_missed: In the default scene nothing but the cube is near the tool, so the first grasp point was always clear and the grasp was never checked against clutter.
fix: Choose the grasp point along the handle (candidates 2.5-12.5 cm from the free end) as the first one whose vertical approach is clear: the hand box plus the open-finger box is checked against get_obstacles() (the tool itself excluded). The grasp height comes from the perceived tool pose (grip_z = tool z) and the lift height from max(0.15, tool z + 0.12). If the chosen point is not the usual one, set the tool down at a nearby free spot (footprint checked with the tool's rotation) and regrasp it at the usual point, so the rest of the program (test lift, carry or slide, hook placement) runs unchanged. Seeds 0-9: 1.0 on every scene; held-out seeds 100-119: 1.0 everywhere except v6 (0.95).
general_rule: Before grasping, check the approach of the gripper (hand and open fingers) for clutter at several candidate grasp points and take the first clear one; if that grasp is unsuitable for using the object, use it only to move the object to free space, then regrasp properly.
